stem: When assessing a toddler for foreign body aspiration, what is the most common finding on an expiratory chest radiograph?

options.text: Complete collapse of the lung distal to the object
Increased lung volume and lucency on the affected side due to air trapping
A large pleural effusion on the side of the aspiration
Silhouette sign obscuring the right heart border

explanation: Increased lung volume and lucency on the affected side due to air trapping is the typical expiratory radiographic finding in foreign body aspiration. The foreign body acts as a one-way valve, allowing air in but limiting air out.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect because complete collapse is not the most common expiratory finding in toddler foreign body aspiration; air trapping is more typical.
optionExplanations.B: Correct because the foreign body can act as a one-way valve, so the affected lung becomes overinflated and more lucent on expiration due to air trapping.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because a pleural effusion suggests another process, such as infection or inflammation, rather than the usual finding of foreign body aspiration.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because the silhouette sign is associated with adjacent consolidation or soft tissue opacity, not the air trapping seen with a foreign body.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because the usual finding is unilateral air trapping on the affected side, not diffuse bilateral hyperinflation.

source.hint: Focus on what happens to trapped air when the child tries to breathe out.
